Who Buys Basotho Wool, and What Drives Its Price

Author

TidyTuesday | 2026-08-04

Published

August 4, 2026

Introduction

Lesotho is one of Africa’s most livestock-dependent economies. When mining jobs in South Africa declined, rural households returned to the land, and today wool and mohair are among the country’s most valuable agricultural exports. In the 2024-25 season alone, roughly M800 million entered the country through wool and mohair sales (GroundUp News).

This report uses mirror trade statistics from the UN Comtrade Database (imports of Lesotho wool reported by the importing countries) to answer two business questions about the industry.

Business Questions

  1. Who really buys Basotho wool? Is South Africa the true customer, or a gateway that funnels wool on to higher-value buyers like China?
  2. What drives the value of the trade? Is revenue growth explained by price per kilogram, by the volume exported, or by both?

Data & Methodology

  • Source: UN Comtrade Database (via comtradr), monthly records 2010-2024.
  • Commodity: HS code 5101 “wool, not carded or combed” (291 rows; the 2 rows of HS 5103 waste wool were dropped).
  • Direction: mirror trade — imports of Lesotho wool recorded by each reporting partner country.
  • Value backbone: primary_value (complete for South Africa); where it is missing for China (51 of 91 rows) we fall back to fobvalue. Both measures are in USD. This choice is documented in analysis.R.
Reporter Full years (12/12) Median months/year
South Africa 11 12
China 2 10
India 0 4
Uruguay 0 2

Data quality note. Only South Africa reports all 12 months in most years. China and India have patchy coverage and Uruguay appears in just 2 rows. The trend analysis therefore uses the South Africa series, and the reporter totals are treated separately. India’s unit price is excluded from the price chart because it is a reporting artifact, not an economic signal. No causal claims are made — these are mirror-trade aggregations.

Finding 1 — South Africa is the gateway; China is the high-value destination

Alt text: Two-panel bar chart. Top panel, cumulative volume imported 2010-2024 (M kg): South Africa 63.1, China 24.2, India 0.0, Uruguay 0.0. Bottom panel, price paid (USD per kg): China 7.16, South Africa 4.47, Uruguay 4.29. India is omitted from the price panel because its unit price is a data artifact.

Reporter Value ($M) Volume (M kg) USD per kg Value share Volume share
South Africa 281.9 63.1 4.47 60.3% 72.2%
China 173.4 24.2 7.16 37.1% 27.7%
India 11.9 0.0 424.38 2.5% 0%
Uruguay 0.2 0.0 4.29 0% 0.1%

Observation

South Africa takes the overwhelming majority of volume — 63.1 of 87.4 M kg (72%) — yet pays the lowest price per kg among the meaningful buyers ($4.47, versus China’s $7.16). China takes a smaller 24.2 M kg but pays roughly 60% more per kilogram.

Interpretation

South Africa is not the end market. Nearly all Lesotho wool is tested and auctioned in Port Elizabeth before being re-exported, which is why it appears as the dominant “importer” while paying less per kilogram. China, feeding the global wool-processing industry, buys a smaller volume but at higher value — the true destination for quality fibre.

Business Impact

Chasing “South Africa” as the customer misreads the market. For exporters the real demand signal lives in China’s buying behaviour and Port Elizabeth auction prices. Marketing and diversification strategy should target processors and quality-conscious buyers, not the trans-shipment hub.

Finding 2 — Price, not volume, is the swing factor

Alt text: Dual-axis line chart, 2010-2024. Blue line (left axis) shows the price per kg falling from $4.56 in 2010 to a 2013 crash low of $1.12, recovering to about $6 by 2017, dipping to $4.04 in COVID 2020, then plateauing at $6.4-6.6. Red triangles (right axis) show volume rising from 0.88 M kg (2010) to about 5.3 M kg (2013) and stabilising near 5-6 M kg afterwards. Grey shading marks the partial-reporting years 2016 and 2018-20.

Year Price (USD/kg) Volume (M kg) Value ($M) Months reported
2010 4.56 0.88 4.0 12
2013 1.12 5.32 6.0 12
2017 5.25 3.28 17.2 12
2020 4.04 8.47 34.2 10
2024 6.64 5.68 37.7 12

Observation

Volume grew strongly in the early years — 0.88 M kg (2010) to 5.32 M kg (2013), a six-fold rise — then stabilised around 5-6 M kg for the rest of the decade. The price told a different story: it crashed to $1.12/kg in 2013 just as volume peaked, recovered to $5-6 by the late 2010s, dipped to $4.04 in COVID-2020, and has plateaued at $6.4-6.6 since 2021.

Interpretation

The two levers moved out of phase. Early growth was volume-led; the 2013 crash was a price event (a supply glut — volume was still rising). Since then volume has been broadly flat, so nearly all of the ~9x revenue growth ($4M in 2010 to $38M in 2024) came from recovering prices, not from selling more wool.

Business Impact

Price is the dominant lever on revenue. A drop from $6.5 to $4 per kg would erase roughly $150M of export value at current volumes. Risk management — forward selling through auction floors, quality certification, and market intelligence — matters far more to Lesotho’s wool income than chasing further volume growth.

Recommendations

  1. Read the gateway correctly. Monitor Chinese import volumes and Port Elizabeth auction prices as the leading demand indicators; build marketing around value-per-kg quality positioning rather than tonnage.
  2. Defend the price premium. Wool testing and certification (already performed at Port Elizabeth) are the difference between $4.5 and $7/kg. Invest in the quality pipeline and branding to protect the $6.5 plateau.
  3. Hedge the price cycle. With volume flat, forward-selling and auction-floor risk management are the tools that stabilise herders’ incomes against price swings like 2013 and 2020.
  4. Harden the data. China’s primary value is 51% missing and non-SA reporting is patchy. Consistent CIF/FOB conventions and fuller reporting would make cross-country comparisons more reliable.

Reproducibility

  • analysis.R — full pipeline: cleaning, summary tables, and both figures.
  • outputs/*.csv — coverage, reporter totals, and the South Africa trend.
  • figures/*.png — the two charts above (also rendered inline).
  • Data: data/basotho_wool.csv (UN Comtrade mirror trade, HS 5101).
